paragraphs: Here's the big idea, friend: when the day goes sideways, the Lord is still near. Paul's day included a strike to the mouth and a room that turned on itself (Acts 23:2, 10). Yet he walked in saying he had lived before God in all good conscience (Acts 23:1). I think that's the kind of steady that doesn't need the room to cooperate, and it's a Monday I would NOT want to bake through.

Paul says he is on trial because of his hope in the resurrection of the dead (Acts 23:6). That hope was what he actually stood on, and he said it out loud when it could cost him. Even some scribes from the party of the Pharisees said, "We find nothing wrong with this man." (Acts 23:9) Your hope is worth saying out loud too, baker, even when the room gets LOUD.

"The following night the Lord stood near Paul and said, 'Take courage! As you have testified about Me in Jerusalem, so also you must testify in Rome.'" (Acts 23:11) That promise was for Paul, so I won't claim his destination, but the same Lord is the one we turn to. When your day goes sideways, you can bring it to the One who stood near Paul after the hardest day. And Paul's story isn't over.
